questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic hypertension is started on an investigational oral antihypertensive drug. The research team wants to assess the overall amount of drug that successfully reaches systemic circulation and is available to the target tissues over a given time period. Which of the following pharmacokinetic parameters would best reflect this?

options.label: D
options.text: Area under the blood concentration–time curve (AUC)

questions.answerText: Area under the blood concentration–time curve (AUC)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Area under the blood concentration–time curve (AUC)

 

AUC represents the total exposure of the body to the drug after administration and is the most reliable measure of the amount of drug that reaches systemic circulation (bioavailability).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Volume of distribution (Vd): Volume of distribution (Vd) is a theoretical parameter describing how a drug distributes between plasma and tissues but does not measure the amount of drug actually absorbed into the body.

 

Option B. Time-to-peak blood concentration: Tmax (Time-to-peak concentration) reflects the rate of absorption but does not indicate how much drug ultimately reaches systemic circulation.

 

Option C. Peak (maximum) blood concentration: Cmax (Peak concentration) only shows the maximum level achieved at one time point, not the overall exposure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) is the best pharmacokinetic measure of the total amount of drug reaching systemic circulation and tissues over time following oral administration, while Cmax, Tmax, and Vd provide information about rate of absorption, peak levels, and distribution, respectively.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man is enrolled in a pharmacokinetic trial for a new oral antiplatelet drug. After administration, serial blood samples are obtained and plotted to create a concentration–time curve. The investigators also administer the drug intravenously on a separate occasion and repeat the sampling. They then calculate the ratio of the area under the curve (AUC) after oral administration to the AUC after intravenous administration. Which of the following pharmacokinetic parameters is being measured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Bioavailability

 

Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of an administered dose of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation. It is calculated as the ratio of AUC (oral) to AUC (IV), since IV dosing gives 100% bioavailability.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clearance: Clearance represents the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time, determined by metabolism and excretion, not by comparing AUCs of oral vs. IV routes.

 

Option B. Extraction ratio: Extraction ratio is the fraction of drug removed by an organ during its passage (e.g., hepatic extraction ratio), not related to oral vs. IV AUC comparison.

 

Option C. Absorption: Absorption refers to the process of drug entry into the bloodstream from the site of administration but does not directly quantify systemic exposure relative to IV dosing.

 

Educational Objective:


Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation, best measured by the ratio of the area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) for oral administration compared with intravenous administration.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is given an experimental acidic drug (pKa = 4.4) orally. The gastric pH is 2.4, and plasma pH is 7.4. The drug crosses biological membranes only by passive diffusion, without any transporters. Which of the following observations regarding the drug’s absorption and distribution is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The drug will be hydrolyzed by reaction with gastric HCl and therefore cannot be absorbed

options.label: B
options.text: In plasma, the ratio of the ionized drug form will be about 1000 times higher than the nonionized form

options.label: C
options.text: The drug will not be absorbed unless gastric pH is raised to equal the pKa (e.g., with antacids)

options.label: D
options.text: Only the ionized form of the drug will be absorbed across membranes into plasma

questions.answerText: In plasma, the ratio of the ionized drug form will be about 1000 times higher than the nonionized form
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) In plasma, the ratio of the ionized drug form will be about 1000 times higher than the nonionized form

 

For a weak acid, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation applies: pH = pKa + log (ionized/nonionized). At plasma pH 7.4, with pKa 4.4 → ratio = 10^(7.4−4.4) = 1000:1 → drug is mainly ionized in plasma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The drug will be hydrolyzed by reaction with gastric HCl and therefore cannot be absorbed: Incorrect. Acidic drugs are not destroyed or hydrolyzed by gastric HCl; aspirin and similar weak acids are absorbed well from the stomach and intestine.

 

Option C. The drug will not be absorbed unless gastric pH is raised to equal the pKa (e.g., with antacids): Incorrect. Drug absorption does not require pH to be equal to pKa. At pH = pKa, drug is 50% ionized, which is actually less favorable than at lower gastric pH where more of the drug remains nonionized and absorbable.

 

Option D. Only the ionized form of the drug will be absorbed across membranes into plasma: Incorrect. Nonionized forms are preferentially absorbed by passive diffusion; ionized forms are poorly membrane-permeable.

 

Educational Objective:


Weak acids are best absorbed in the stomach because the low pH keeps them in the nonionized, lipid-soluble form. In plasma (higher pH), weak acids exist mostly in the ionized form (≈1000:1 ionized:nonionized at pH 7.4 vs. pKa 4.4), explaining ion trapping and reduced diffusion across membranes.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with septic shock is started on a constant-rate intravenous infusion of an investigational antibiotic via an infusion pump. The team wants to predict how long it will take before the patient’s plasma drug concentration reaches steady state (Css). Which of the following pharmacokinetic factors determines the time required to achieve steady state?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Half-life (t½)

 

The time to reach steady state depends only on the elimination half-life of the drug, not on the dose or infusion rate. It takes about 4–5 half-lives to reach ≈94–97% of Css.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Infusion rate (mg/min): Determines what the steady-state concentration will be (Css = infusion rate / clearance), but does not affect how quickly steady state is reached.

 

Option B. Apparent volume of distribution (Vd): Affects half-life indirectly (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL), but by itself does not directly dictate the time course to steady state.

 

Option D. Clearance (CL): Like Vd, clearance helps determine the value of half-life and Css, but the actual “clock” to reach steady state is governed by half-life.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The time to reach steady-state plasma concentration (Css) during constant infusion depends solely on the drug’s elimination half-life (≈4–5 t½), not on infusion rate, clearance, or volume of distribution.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed an NSAID for long-term suppression of joint inflammation. The drug has the following pharmacokinetic properties: Bioavailability (F) = 1.0 (100%)Plasma half-life (t½) = 6.93 hVolume of distribution (Vd) = 100 L To maintain adequate anti-inflammatory activity, the desired average steady-state plasma concentration (Css,avg) is 5 mg/L. The drug will be administered orally 4 times daily. What should be the required single oral dose to achieve the target concentration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 300 mg

 

Stepwise Calculation:

 

1. Convert Css to consistent units:


5 mcg/mL = 5 mg/L

 

2. Clearance (CL):

 

CL=0.693×Vdt1/2CL=t1/2​0.693×Vd​CL=0.693×1006.93≈10 L/hCL=6.930.693×100​≈10L/h

 

3. Maintenance Dose Rate (mg/h):

 

Dose Rate=Css×CLDose Rate=Css×CL=5 mg/L×10 L/h=50 mg/h=5mg/L×10L/h=50mg/h

 

4. Dose per dosing interval:

 

Dose = Dose Rate × Dosing interval 

 

Dose rate = 50 mg/h

 

Dosing interval is 4 times a day means after 6 hours

 

Dose = 50×6=300 mg

 

Answer: 300 mg

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a long history of severe motion sickness is scheduled to go on a cruise and asks for preventive therapy. You consider prescribing scopolamine transdermal patches. Which of the following comorbid conditions would represent the most important contraindication because of high risk of adverse effects?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Angle-closure glaucoma

 

Scopolamine is an antimuscarinic drug. Antimuscarinics cause mydriasis (pupil dilation), which can obstruct aqueous humor outflow through an already-narrow angle, precipitating acute angle-closure glaucoma—a dangerous and vision-threatening emergency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bradycardia: Scopolamine usually causes tachycardia (via vagolytic effect), so bradycardia is not a contraindication; in fact, it might be partly offset.

 

Option B. Parkinson’s disease: Antimuscarinics like trihexyphenidyl are sometimes used to treat tremor in Parkinson’s; scopolamine is not a treatment, but Parkinson’s itself is not a contraindication.

 

Option C. Hypothyroidism: This condition has no major interaction with antimuscarinic drugs.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Antimuscarinic drugs such as scopolamine can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma by inducing mydriasis and blocking aqueous humor outflow; therefore, narrow-angle glaucoma is a key contraindication to their use.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman receives bethanechol after abdominal surgery to stimulate bowel motility. Shortly after administration, she develops a mild fall in heart rate and new-onset wheezing. Which of the following best explains these observed responses?

options.label: C
options.text: Expected side effects of the drug

questions.answerText: Expected side effects of the drug
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Expected side effects of the drug

 

Bethanechol is a direct muscarinic agonist (cholinomimetic). By stimulating M2 receptors in the heart, it slows heart rate, and by stimulating M3 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, it causes bronchoconstriction (wheezing). These are expected parasympathomimetic effects, not evidence of a new pathology.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reflex (baroreceptor) suppression of cardiac rate: Reflex bradycardia (via baroreceptors) occurs when blood pressure rises; bethanechol generally lowers BP slightly due to vasodilation, so bradycardia here is direct muscarinic effect, not reflex.

 

Option B. Parasympathetic ganglionic activation: Bethanechol acts directly on muscarinic receptors; it does not activate nicotinic receptors in ganglia, so “parasympathetic ganglionic activation” is incorrect.

 

Option D. Undiagnosed asthma: While bethanechol could worsen asthma, the described wheezing after drug administration is a predictable muscarinic effect, not necessarily undiagnosed asthma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bethanechol, a direct muscarinic agonist, produces predictable parasympathomimetic side effects such as bradycardia (M2) and bronchoconstriction (M3). These effects are expected, not due to reflexes, ganglionic activation, or occult disease.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the ED with severe hypertension (200/140 mmHg), tachycardia (≈130/min), headaches, diaphoresis, and palpitations. He is mistakenly treated with a large IV dose of propranolol before the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma is recognized. Which of the following is the most likely outcome if a pure β-blocker is given without α-blockade?

options.label: A
options.text: Restoration of normal sinus rhythm but no blood pressure change

options.label: B
options.text: Heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and death

options.label: C
options.text: Sudden and marked increase in blood pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Normalization of blood pressure but persistent tachycardia

questions.answerText: Sudden and marked increase in blood pressure
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Sudden and marked increase in blood pressure 

 

Blocking β2 receptors in vascular smooth muscle removes vasodilatory tone, leaving unopposed α1-mediated vasoconstriction from catecholamine excess → hypertensive crisis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Restoration of normal sinus rhythm but no blood pressure change: Wrong because BP will rise, not stay the same.

 

Option B. Heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and death: Heart failure/cardiogenic shock is not the immediate danger; the crisis is uncontrolled vasoconstriction and hypertension.

 

Option D. Normalization of blood pressure but persistent tachycardia: Incorrect, because BP cannot normalize with pure β-blockade; instead, HR may slow but BP worsens.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In pheochromocytoma, giving a nonselective β-blocker without prior α-blockade causes unopposed α1 stimulation → hypertensive crisis. Always start with α-blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) before β-blockade.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old farm worker with organophosphate (AChE inhibitor) poisoning is given an effective dose of atropine to control muscarinic symptoms. Which structure will remain overactivated by excess ACh despite atropine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Skeletal muscle

 

Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only; nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction remain overstimulated by excess ACh.

 

Other Options:

 

Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist, so muscarinic-mediated effects (salivation/lacrimation — salivary and lacrimal glands; bronchoconstriction — airway smooth muscle; bradycardia via SA node) are reversed by atropine. Skeletal muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction is mediated by nicotinic (Nm) receptors, which atropine does not block — therefore nicotinic overstimulation (fasciculations, weakness, paralysis) will persist after atropine administration.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In AChE-inhibitor poisoning, atropine relieves muscarinic symptoms but does not affect nicotinic (skeletal muscle and ganglionic) overstimulation; nicotinic effects require agents like pralidoxime (2-PAM) to restore AChE or other supportive measures.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 5-cm skin laceration on the forearm after a fall. The physician prepares to suture the wound and infiltrates the edges with lidocaine combined with a small amount of epinephrine. What is the most likely reason for adding epinephrine?

options.label: A
options.text: To counteract cardiac depression caused by the anesthetic

options.label: B
options.text: To prevent anaphylaxis in patients who are allergic to the anesthetic

options.label: C
options.text: To reduce the risk of toxicity caused by systemic absorption of the anesthetic

options.label: D
options.text: To shorten the duration of anesthetic action

questions.answerText: To reduce the risk of toxicity caused by systemic absorption of the anesthetic
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) To reduce the risk of toxicity caused by systemic absorption of the anesthetic

 

Epinephrine is added to local anesthetics because its α1-mediated vasoconstriction reduces local blood flow, which both limits systemic absorption (thus decreasing toxicity) and prolongs the duration of local anesthetic action. 

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. To counteract cardiac depression caused by the anesthetic: Incorrect because epinephrine does not counteract the intrinsic cardiac depression of local anesthetics; in fact, it may increase arrhythmia risk. 

 

Option B. To prevent anaphylaxis in patients who are allergic to the anesthetic:  Wrong since epinephrine does not prevent allergic reactions; true allergies (rare, often with ester anesthetics like procaine) require avoidance or substitution, not prophylaxis. 

 

Option D. To shorten the duration of anesthetic action: It is the opposite of the actual effect — epinephrine prolongs, not shortens, anesthetic duration.

questions.stem: In which of the following situations would administration of a non selective beta blocker is considered appropriate and safe?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thyroid storm

 

Nonselective β-blockers such as propranolol are used in acute symptomatic hyperthyroidism because they alleviate adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety) and at high doses also inhibit peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Severe acute congestive heart failure: Contraindicated: β-blockers decrease myocardial contractility, worsening decompensated CHF.

 

Option C. Bradycardia: Contraindicated: β-blockade worsens bradyarrhythmia.

 

Option d. Asthma: Contraindicated: Nonselective β-blockers block β2 receptors, precipitating bronchospasm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nonselective β-blockers are contraindicated in asthma, bradycardia, and acute decompensated heart failure, but are highly effective and appropriate in the management of acute symptomatic hyperthyroidism, where they control adrenergic symptoms and reduce T3 formation.

questions.stem: Pindolol is a β blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA). Which of the following best describes its pharmacological action?

options.label: A
options.text: Useful when cardiac positive inotropic and chronotropic effects are wanted

options.label: C
options.text: Potentiates the actions of norepinephrine on α-adrenergic receptors

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Is a partial agonist 

 

Acebutolol and pindolol act as β receptor antagonists with weak agonist activity. At rest, their partial agonist action prevents profound bradycardia and negative inotropy. During high sympathetic drive, they block the receptor from full stimulation by catecholamines, hence acting like antagonists.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Useful when cardiac positive inotropic and chronotropic effects are wanted: Incorrect. β blockers with ISA have some agonist activity but are primarily used when we want to avoid excessive bradycardia or negative inotropy (e.g., in patients with borderline bradycardia). They are not chosen when we desire strong cardiac stimulation; in fact, β agonists like dobutamine would be used in such cases.

 

Option C. Potentiates the actions of norepinephrine on α-adrenergic receptors: Incorrect. ISA has nothing to do with α receptor potentiation. This description fits drugs that might increase norepinephrine availability (e.g., reuptake inhibitors), not β blockers with ISA.

 

Option D. Causes norepinephrine and epinephrine release: Incorrect. β blockers with ISA do not enhance catecholamine release. On the contrary, they partially mimic their effect at β receptors while preventing full agonist stimulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

β blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA), such as acebutolol and pindolol, act as partial agonists at β receptors. They prevent excessive bradycardia and negative inotropy at rest but block full sympathetic stimulation during stress. They are not associated with catecholamine release, α potentiation, or intentional cardiac stimulation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine at night for allergic rhinitis. The next morning she feels drowsy, has a dry mouth, and complains of urinary hesitancy. On review of her medications, her physician notes that many first-generation H1 antihistamines, typical antipsychotics, and tricyclic antidepressants share a common adverse effect profile. These side effects most closely resemble those produced by which of the following drugs?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Atropine

 

First-generation H1 blockers, phenothiazines, and tricyclic antidepressants all have significant antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) actions in addition to their primary effects. This leads to dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and sedation — closely mimicking atropine toxicity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bethanechol: Incorrect. Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist that stimulates bladder contraction and GI motility. Its effects are opposite to the anticholinergic side effects of first-generation H1 blockers.

 

Option C. Neostigmine: Incorrect. An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases cholinergic transmission, causing bradycardia, salivation, diarrhea, and miosis — again opposite to the effects of H1 blockers and TCAs.

 

Option D. Propranolol: Incorrect. A nonselective β-blocker; causes bradycardia and bronchoconstriction but has no antimuscarinic effects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

First-generation H1 antihistamines, phenothiazines, and tricyclic antidepressants share prominent antimuscarinic properties that account for many of their side effects (sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision). Their adverse effect profile most closely resembles that of atropine.

questions.stem: While volunteering in a resource-limited hospital, you need an IV inotrope for acute cardiac failure but dobutamine is unavailable. Which of the following alternative drug choices or combinations would most closely reproduce dobutamine’s β1 inotropic action without causing problematic α₁-mediated vasoconstriction?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Norepinephrine plus phentolamine

 

Dobutamine’s desired effect in acute heart failure is predominant β1 stimulation (↑contractility) with minimal α₁ vasoconstriction. Norepinephrine itself stimulates both α₁ and β₁; if you pharmacologically block α₁ with phentolamine, the net effect is mainly β1 inotropy — approximating dobutamine’s inotropic action (though clinically the combination is awkward and requires tight control). Ephedrine (E) is a mixed direct/indirect sympathomimetic that raises heart rate and contractility but also increases peripheral resistance and is less predictable — not an ideal match. Ephedrine + propranolol (B) is self-defeating because propranolol blocks the β1 effects you want. Dopamine at very high dose (C) produces strong α₁ vasoconstriction (↑afterload) and would worsen cardiac output. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

To mimic dobutamine (a primarily β1 inotrope that increases contractility without marked α₁ vasoconstriction), you need β1 stimulation without unopposed α₁ activity — of the listed choices, combining norepinephrine with an α-blocker (phentolamine) best fits that pharmacologic goal, though it’s not an ideal or commonly used clinical substitute and requires careful titration.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old patient needs an ophthalmic exam that requires pupil dilation (mydriasis) but you must preserve normal accommodation (no cycloplegia). Which of the following topical agents is the best choice?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Phenylephrine

 

Mydriasis without cycloplegia is best achieved by stimulating α₁-mediated contraction of the radial (dilator) iris muscle, leaving the parasympathetic muscarinic control of the ciliary muscle (accommodation) intact. Phenylephrine (a drug with α₁ activity) produces pupil dilation via the dilator muscle while not producing muscarinic blockade of accommodation, so it best meets the requirement. Atropine and homatropine are antimuscarinics that cause both mydriasis and cycloplegia (loss of accommodation) and are therefore unsuitable. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that constricts the pupil (miosis) and enhances accommodation—opposite of the goal. Timolol (a topical β-blocker) reduces intraocular pressure but does not reliably produce mydriasis. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

To dilate the pupil without impairing accommodation, use an α₁-acting sympathomimetic (e.g., epinephrine/phenylephrine). Antimuscarinics (atropine, homatropine) cause both mydriasis and cycloplegia and therefore do not preserve accommodation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease has been on levodopa therapy. However, he develops nausea, vomiting, and postural hypotension. His neurologist switches him to a fixed-dose combination of levodopa with carbidopa. Which of the following best describes the role of carbidopa in this combination?

options.label: A
options.text: Blocks ACh release in the CNS

options.label: C
options.text: Increases permeability of the blood-brain barrier to levo dopa

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibits metabolic conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS

questions.answerText: Inhibits metabolic conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Inhibits metabolic conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS

 

Carbidopa is a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor, reducing peripheral side effects (nausea, vomiting, hypotension) and increasing levodopa delivery to the brain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blocks ACh release in the CNS: Incorrect. This is the mechanism of central anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine), not carbidopa.

 

Option B. Helps activate dietary vitamin B6: Wrong. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) actually increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa, worsening its efficacy. Carbidopa prevents this by blocking dopa decarboxylase.

 

Option C. Increases permeability of the blood-brain barrier: Incorrect. Levodopa crosses the BBB via LAT transporters; carbidopa has no effect on barrier permeability.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Carbidopa is a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that prevents premature conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS. This increases levodopa bioavailability in the brain while reducing peripheral side effects.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old male, previously healthy, developed recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures 3 months after a traumatic brain injury. He was started on oral phenytoin, with dose titration guided by plasma levels. Initially, the drug showed an elimination half-life of about 24 hours. Currently, he presents with ataxia, nystagmus, diplopia, and confusion. His serum phenytoin concentration is 30 µg/mL (therapeutic range is 10-20 µg/mL). The decision is made to stop further phenytoin dosing until levels return to therapeutic concentrations. Which of the following statements best describes the expected pharmacokinetics and management in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer flumazenil, which will quickly reverse signs and symptoms of phenytoin toxicity but may cause seizures to recur

options.label: B
options.text: Elimination of phenytoin from the plasma will follow zero-order kinetics for several days

options.label: C
options.text: Give phenobarbital to induce the P450 system, thereby hastening phenytoin’s metabolic elimination

options.label: D
options.text: Plasma phenytoin concentrations will fall to 15 mcg/mL, in the middle of the therapeutic range, by the next day

questions.answerText: Elimination of phenytoin from the plasma will follow zero-order kinetics for several days
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elimination of phenytoin from the plasma will follow zero-order kinetics for several days.

 

At therapeutic levels, phenytoin shows first-order kinetics, but once plasma levels rise beyond the capacity of hepatic enzymes (saturable metabolism), elimination shifts to zero-order kinetics. Thus, drug clearance is constant (linear), not dependent on concentration, and toxicity may persist for days.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Flumazenil: This is a benzodiazepine antagonist, useful in benzodiazepine overdose. It has no role in phenytoin toxicity and may actually precipitate seizures.

 

Option C. Phenobarbital enzyme induction: Though phenobarbital is a CYP inducer, enzyme induction takes several days to weeks to manifest, so it cannot acutely hasten phenytoin clearance.

 

Option D. Half-life prediction: Wrong because in toxic range, phenytoin’s half-life is not fixed; it does not decline by 50% in 24 hours. Instead, clearance is slower and unpredictable due to zero-order kinetics.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Phenytoin exhibits dose-dependent pharmacokinetics:

 

  • At low concentrations → first-order kinetics (constant fraction eliminated).
  • At higher, saturating concentrations → zero-order kinetics (constant amount eliminated).
    Thus, toxicity persists longer, and drug accumulation is dangerous because small dose increases can lead to disproportionate plasma level rises.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has been on pharmacotherapy for some neuropsychiatric condition. After a few weeks, he presents with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination of large volumes of clear, dilute urine. Laboratory evaluation shows low urine osmolality with normal serum sodium. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lithium

 

Lithium is a mood stabilizer commonly used in bipolar disorder. A well-known adverse effect is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI), caused by downregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels in renal collecting ducts, leading to impaired renal concentrating ability. Patients present with polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Diazepam: A benzodiazepine used for anxiety/insomnia. Its adverse effects are sedation, dependence, respiratory depression — not polyuria or NDI.

 

Option B. Fluoxetine: An SSRI antidepressant. Side effects include sexual dysfunction, insomnia, and GI upset. It does not cause polyuria/NDI.

 

Option C. Haloperidol: A typical antipsychotic. Side effects include extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia) and hyperprolactinemia. It has no link to NDI.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lithium therapy can lead to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, presenting with polyuria, polydipsia, and dilute urine due to impaired renal response to ADH. This adverse effect is unique to lithium and helps differentiate it from other psychotropic medications.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is being prepared for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The anesthesia team is comparing two inhaled agents. Agent A has a MAC of 2%, while agent B has a MAC of 100%. Based on the MAC values alone, which statement below is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The time to onset of adequate general anesthesia is 50 times longer for Drug B than for Drug A

options.label: B
options.text: Drug A is more soluble in the blood than Drug B

options.label: C
options.text: The concentration of drug in inspired air that is needed to cause adequate surgical anesthesia is higher for Drug B than for Drug A

options.label: D
options.text: Drug A has a longer duration of action than Drug B

questions.answerText: The concentration of drug in inspired air that is needed to cause adequate surgical anesthesia is higher for Drug B than for Drug A
questions.solutionHtml:
>

 

Explanation of all options 

 

MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) is an index of potency for volatile anesthetics: a lower MAC = greater potency (less inspired concentration required), and a higher MAC = less potency (more inspired concentration required). Thus, because B’s MAC (100%) is much higher than A’s (2%), a far higher inspired concentration of B would be required to produce surgical anesthesia, making (C) correct. MAC values alone tell you nothing about blood solubility or duration/onset kinetics, so (B) is incorrect — solubility (blood/gas partition coefficient) determines onset/duration, not MAC. MAC also does not directly quantify analgesia or muscle relaxation (those are separate drug effects and may not correlate with MAC), so (D) is incorrect. Finally, the time to onset depends on uptake/solubility and ventilation, not simply the ratio of MACs, so the claim in (A) is unfounded; you cannot deduce a “50×” difference in onset time from MAC alone.

 

Educational Objective:

 

MAC measures inhaled anesthetic potency (lower MAC = higher potency). From MAC values alone you can infer only relative inspired concentrations required for surgical anesthesia (higher MAC → higher required concentration); you cannot determine onset/duration, blood solubility, or specific analgesic/muscle-relaxant properties.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who has taken fluoxetine for 5 months is treated for a new medical problem and given an additional medication. Shortly afterward she is rushed to the emergency with unstable vital signs, muscle rigidity, myoclonus, hyperreflexia/CNS irritability, altered consciousness, and shivering. Which of the following added drugs is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.label: B
options.text: Midazolam and fentanyl used during endoscopy

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Sumatriptan for migraine

 

The clinical picture describes serotonin syndrome — a life-threatening excess of serotonergic activity often precipitated when an SSRI (like fluoxetine) is combined with another serotonergic agent. 

 

Sumatriptan is a 5-HT1 agonist (a triptan) and can precipitate serotonin syndrome when given with SSRIs, making it the most likely culprit. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Zolpidem for short-term insomnia: It is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic (GABAergic) and does not cause serotonin syndrome.

 

Option B. Midazolam and fentanyl used during endoscopy: Midazolam + fentanyl are sedative/analgesic agents; fentanyl has occasionally been implicated in serotoninergic reactions but the combination is far less likely than a triptan to produce full serotonin syndrome, and midazolam does not contribute.  

 

Option D. Codeine for cough: Codeine is an opioid prodrug primarily causing sedation, respiratory depression, or, rarely, serotonin effects when combined with certain other drugs (e.g., some opioids like tramadol or meperidine are more serotonergic), but codeine is much less likely to cause this syndrome. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia/myoclonus, altered mental status) and commonly occurs when SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine) are combined with other serotonergic drugs — notably triptans (sumatriptan) — so coadministration should be done with caution or avoided.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with Parkinson’s disease has been on treatment for about 1 year. During follow-up, she complains of progressive changes in her skin. On examination, she has mottled, purplish, lacy discoloration over both lower limbs. She denies pruritus or pain. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of her skin changes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Amantadine

 

Amantadine can cause a characteristic side effect called livedo reticularis, a mottled purplish skin discoloration due to dermal blood vessel changes.

 

Used in early Parkinson’s disease, it enhances dopamine release and blocks NMDA receptors. Its classic adverse effect is livedo reticularis, sometimes with ankle edema.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bromocriptine: A dopamine agonist (ergot derivative). Side effects include nausea, vomiting, hypotension, hallucinations, and rarely pulmonary/pericardial fibrosis, but not livedo reticularis.

 

Option C. Levodopa + Carbidopa: Carbidopa reduces peripheral metabolism of levodopa, lowering nausea/vomiting, but doesn’t add skin side effects.

 

Option D. Pramipexole: A non-ergot dopamine agonist. Can cause somnolence, compulsive behaviors, and hypotension — not livedo reticularis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder presents with severe suicidal thoughts. He is stabilized acutely with a drug that provides rapid antidepressant action within hours. However, for long-term management, his psychiatrist explains that this agent is not suitable for maintenance therapy and a more conventional antidepressant will be required. Which of the following statements correctly differentiates the acute vs. long-term use of antidepressants in this setting?

options.label: A
options.text: Esketamine is used for long-term prevention of relapse, while SSRIs are only for rapid control of suicidal ideation

options.label: B
options.text: Esketamine provides rapid symptom relief but is not used for maintenance due to safety and tolerance issues

options.label: C
options.text: SSRIs act within hours while esketamine requires weeks for antidepressant action

options.label: D
options.text: Both esketamine and SSRIs are equally effective for acute suicidal ideation

questions.answerText: Esketamine provides rapid symptom relief but is not used for maintenance due to safety and tolerance issues
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Esketamine provides rapid symptom relief but is not used for maintenance due to safety and tolerance issues

 

Esketamine shows rapid effect (within hours) but carries risks like dissociation, hypertension, abuse potential, hence not used long-term. SSRIs/SNRIs are preferred for maintenance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Esketamine is used for long-term prevention of relapse, while SSRIs are only for rapid control of suicidal ideation: Incorrect. Opposite of truth. SSRIs are maintenance drugs; ketamine is not.

Option D. Both esketamine and SSRIs are equally effective for acute suicidal ideation: Incorrect. Esketamine is clearly superior for acute suicidality, SSRIs are not helpful acutely.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with BP 240/130 mmHg, severe headache, and blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows papilledema. He is diagnosed with hypertensive emergency. His serum creatinine is elevated, suggesting acute renal dysfunction. Which of the following drugs would be most appropriate in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fenoldopam

 

Selective D1 receptor agonist → causes arteriolar vasodilation, increases renal blood flow, natriuresis, and diuresis. Very useful in hypertensive emergency with renal impairment. That’s why this is the best option here.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sodium nitroprusside: Very effective, rapid-acting vasodilator for hypertensive emergencies, but it carries the risk of cyanide toxicity, especially in renal impairment. Hence, not preferred in this patient.

 

Option B. Labetalol: Commonly used in hypertensive emergencies (especially in aortic dissection, pregnancy, and when tachycardia is present). However, it does not improve renal perfusion like fenoldopam.

 

Option D. Nitroglycerine: Mainly venodilator, reduces preload, useful in hypertensive emergencies with myocardial ischemia or pulmonary edema, but not ideal in renal dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painless ulcer on her genitalia for 2 weeks. On examination, she has a clean, indurated ulcer with raised edges and bilateral firm, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is positive, and Treponema pallidum infection is confirmed. She is otherwise healthy and not pregnant. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose

options.label: B
options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 doses

options.label: C
options.text: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV for 14 days

options.label: D
options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days

questions.answerText: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose

 

For primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis (<1 year duration), this is the drug of choice.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 doses: Incorrect here, but correct for late latent syphilis (>1 year duration) or syphilis of unknown duration.

 

Option C. Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV for 14 days: Incorrect. This is reserved for neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis.

 

Option D. Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days: Incorrect here, but a valid alternative for penicillin-allergic patients in primary/secondary syphilis.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man visits a pharmacy and requests ciprofloxacin without a prescription, stating he has taken it before for urinary infection. The pharmacist refuses, stating that dispensing this drug without a doctor’s prescription is illegal, as it is regulated under a particular drug schedule. Which drug schedule does ciprofloxacin fall under in India?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Schedule H

 

Most prescription-only drugs (antibiotics, antituberculars, etc.) fall under Schedule H, and ciprofloxacin is one of them. Dispensing without prescription is illegal.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Schedule G: Incorrect. These are drugs to be taken only under medical supervision (e.g., hormones, hypoglycemics). They require a label warning but can be dispensed with a prescription. Ciprofloxacin is not here.

 

Option C. Schedule X: Incorrect. This includes certain habit-forming drugs like barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, which need special prescription and record-keeping for 2 years.

 

Option D. Schedule C: Incorrect. This includes biological and special products like vaccines, sera, toxins, insulin.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding thalidomide are correct? Cereblon (CRBN) binding explains its teratogenic effect leading to phocomeliaIt is used in erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) and multiple myelomaIt commonly causes peripheral neuropathy and diarrhoeaIt acts by decreasing the action of TNF-α and IL-6
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1, 2 and 4 only

 

1. Cereblon (CRBN) binding explains its teratogenic effect leading to phocomelia (True): Thalidomide binds to CRBN, altering E3 ubiquitin ligase function, disrupting fetal limb development → phocomelia.

 

2. It is used in erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) and multiple myeloma (True): Main indications = erythema nodosum leprosum (anti-inflammatory) and multiple myeloma (anti-angiogenic, immunomodulatory).

 

4. It acts by decreasing the action of TNF-α and IL-6 (True): Its immunomodulatory action includes ↓ TNF-α, ↓ IL-6, ↓ IL-12 → reduced inflammation and anti-myeloma effects.

 

Incorrect Statement:

 

3. It commonly causes peripheral neuropathy and diarrhoea (False): Thalidomide causes peripheral neuropathy (common dose-limiting toxicity) but constipation (not diarrhoea) due to anti-cholinergic + sedative effects.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, chills, and rigors after returning from a 3-week trip to Nigeria. Peripheral smear confirms Plasmodium falciparum infection. The physician considers various antimalarial drugs, some of which act as erythrocytic schizonticides (killing parasites in red blood cells), while others target tissue or gametocyte stages. Which of the following drugs act as erythrocytic schizonticides? ArtesunateChloroquineLumefantrinePrimaquine
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1, 2 and 3 only

 

1. Artesunate (True): Artemisinin derivative; rapid-acting blood schizonticide, especially effective against falciparum erythrocytic stages.

 

2. Chloroquine (True): Classical erythrocytic schizonticide, though resistance is widespread in falciparum.

 

3. Lumefantrine (True): Partner drug with artemether in ACT; acts as a blood schizonticide on falciparum.

 

Incorrect Statement:

 

4. Primaquine (False): Not an erythrocytic schizonticide. It is a tissue schizonticide (kills hypnozoites of vivax/ovale) and gametocytocide.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on chronic hemodialysis presents with progressive fatigue, pallor, and decreased exercise tolerance. Laboratory investigations show: Hemoglobin: 7.8 g/dLMCV: 88 fLReticulocyte count: LowSerum ferritin: NormalVitamin B12 and folate levels: Normal He is started on a therapy that increases his hemoglobin gradually over the next few weeks. Two months later, his blood pressure rises significantly, requiring antihypertensive adjustment. Which of the following statements about the drug used in this patient is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It acts via JAK2/STAT signaling after binding to receptors on erythroid progenitor cells

options.label: B
options.text: Its endogenous counterpart is produced mainly by Kupffer cells of the liver in adults

options.label: C
options.text: Its use is associated with megaloblastic anemia due to folate depletion

options.label: D
options.text: It is indicated only when serum ferritin is less than 15 ng/mL

questions.answerText: It acts via JAK2/STAT signaling after binding to receptors on erythroid progenitor cells
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) It acts via JAK2/STAT signaling after binding to receptors on erythroid progenitor cells


Erythropoietin binds to its receptor on erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow, activating the JAK2/STAT pathway, promoting proliferation and differentiation → ↑ RBC production.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Its endogenous counterpart is produced mainly by Kupffer cells of the liver in adults: Incorrect. In adults, EPO is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the kidney. The fetal liverproduces EPO in utero.

 

Option C. Its use is associated with megaloblastic anemia due to folate depletion: Incorrect. EPO does not cause folate deficiency. The adverse effects are hypertension, thrombosis, flu-like symptoms, and risk of pure red cell aplasia (rare, antibody-mediated).

 

Option D. It is indicated only when serum ferritin is less than 15 ng/mL: Incorrect. EPO is used in anemia of chronic kidney disease, but it requires adequate iron stores. Ferritin < 15 indicates severe iron deficiency, where iron therapy (not EPO alone) is indicated.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing ischemic heart disease presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and ankle edema. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and heart rate 78/min. Echocardiography shows LVEF = 30%. He has been optimized with loop diuretics for symptom relief. Which of the following drugs improve survival (mortality benefit) in patients with HFrEF (Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction)? Sacubitril-valsartan CombinationCarvedilolFurosemideEplerenoneEmpagliflozin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1, 2, 4 and 5 only

 

Drugs that Reduce Mortality in HFrEF (Heart Failure with reduced EF, LVEF ≤40%)

 

1. RAAS Blockers

 

  • ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril)
  • ARBs (losartan, valsartan, candesartan) – if ACEI not tolerated
  • ARNI (sacubitril + valsartan) – preferred over ACEI/ARB now → superior mortality benefit

 

2. Beta-Blockers (specific evidence-based ones only)

 

  • Carvedilol
  • Metoprolol succinate (ER)
  • Bisoprolol
  • Others (atenolol, propranolol) do not improve survival in HFrEF.

 

4. SGLT2 Inhibitors

 

  • Dapagliflozin
  • Empagliflozin
  • Mortality + hospitalization benefit in HFrEF (even in non-diabetics).

 

5. Other agents with mortality benefit (special situations)

 

  • Hydralazine + Isosorbide dinitrate → mortality benefit in Black patients with HFrEF or patients intolerant to ACEI/ARB.

 

3. Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRAs)

 

  • Spironolactone
  • Eplerenone
  • Reduce mortality and hospitalization by countering aldosterone’s harmful remodeling effects.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with dysuria, urgency, and frequency for 2 days. She has no fever, flank pain, diabetes, or prior urological problems. Urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Which of the following is the most appropriate single-dose treatment for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Fosfomycin

 

Fosfomycin trometamol 3 g orally as a single dose is recommended as a first-line regimen for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women. Very effective, convenient, and avoids resistance issues seen with fluoroquinolones.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Nitrofurantoin: Incorrect. Nitrofurantoin is first-line for uncomplicated cystitis but requires a 5–7 day course, not a single dose.

 

Option C. Norfloxacin: Incorrect. A fluoroquinolone. Not recommended as first-line for uncomplicated cystitis due to high resistance rates and significant toxicity (tendinopathy, QT prolongation, neuropathy).

 

Option D. Ceftriaxone: Incorrect. IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin, used in complicated UTI or pyelonephritis. Not appropriate for an otherwise healthy young woman with simple cystitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Single-dose treatment of uncomplicated cystitis = Fosfomycin.
  • Nitrofurantoin is also first-line, but needs a multi-day course.
  • Fluoroquinolones and parenteral cephalosporins are not first-line for simple cystitis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and statin intolerance due to myopathy is started on a new oral drug that lowers LDL-C by ~20%. This agent is a prodrug activated only in the liver (not in muscle), thereby reducing the risk of myopathy. After 3 months of therapy, his lipid profile shows significant LDL reduction, but he develops gout-like symptoms. Which of the following statements regarding this drug is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, preventing cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes

options.label: B
options.text: It inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol biosynthesis

options.label: C
options.text: It blocks NPC1L1 transporter in the intestinal brush border, preventing cholesterol absorption

options.label: D
options.text: It enhances LDL receptor recycling by inhibiting PCSK9

questions.answerText: It inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol biosynthesis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol biosynthesis

 

Bempedoic acid is a prodrug activated by ACSVL1 enzyme in the liver. It inhibits ATP citrate lyase, decreasing cholesterol synthesis → ↓ LDL-C ~18–20%. No activation in muscle → less risk of myopathy. Adverse effect: hyperuricemia/gout.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, preventing cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes: Incorrect.This is the mechanism of statins. Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase, so it is not a statin.

 

Option C. It blocks NPC1L1 transporter in the intestinal brush border, preventing cholesterol absorption: Incorrect. This is the mechanism of ezetimibe, not bempedoic acid.

 

Option D. It enhances LDL receptor recycling by inhibiting PCSK9: Incorrect. This is the mechanism of alirocumab, evolocumab (PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies) or inclisiran (siRNA PCSK9 inhibitor).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Oral, liver-activated prodrug → safe in statin-intolerant patients.
  • Mechanism: ATP citrate lyase inhibition (upstream of statins).
  • Adverse effect: hyperuricemia, tendon rupture (rare).
  • LDL reduction: ~20% (less than statins, more than ezetimibe alone).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has a history of depressive episodes and one prior suicide attempt. He is currently in remission on mood stabilizer therapy. Among the following agents used in bipolar disorder, which drug has the strongest evidence for reducing the risk of suicide?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lithium

 

Lithium is the only mood stabilizer with consistent, strong evidence for reducing suicide risk in patients with bipolar disorder. It decreases both suicidal ideation and completed suicides, beyond its mood-stabilizing effect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Fluoxetine: Incorrect. An SSRI antidepressant; may be used in bipolar depression (with an antimanic agent, e.g., fluoxetine + olanzapine combo). However, SSRIs do not reduce suicide risk and can sometimes increase risk of switch to mania.

 

Option C. Lamotrigine: Incorrect. Useful in preventing bipolar depressive relapses, but no proven anti-suicidal benefit.

 

Option D. Clozapine: Incorrect (in bipolar). Clozapine has proven anti-suicidal effect in schizophrenia (InterSePT trial), but not in bipolar disorder. Hence not the correct choice here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Bipolar disorder → Lithium reduces suicide risk.
  • Schizophrenia → Clozapine reduces suicide risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia with rocuronium as the neuromuscular blocking agent. At the end of surgery, the anesthesiologist considers reversal of residual neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following statements regarding reversal agents is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Neostigmine reverses rocuronium by direct encapsulation, while sugammadex works by acetylcholinesterase inhibition

options.label: B
options.text: Sugammadex can reverse profound rocuronium-induced blockade within 2–3 minutes, unlike neostigmine which requires partial spontaneous recovery

options.label: C
options.text: Neostigmine is safer in patients with severe bradycardia, whereas sugammadex requires co-administration of atropine or glycopyrrolate

options.label: D
options.text: Both sugammadex and neostigmine are equally effective against benzylisoquinolinium agents like atracurium

questions.answerText: Sugammadex can reverse profound rocuronium-induced blockade within 2–3 minutes, unlike neostigmine which requires partial spontaneous recovery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sugammadex can reverse profound rocuronium-induced blockade within 2–3 minutes, unlike neostigmine which requires partial spontaneous recovery

 

  • Sugammadex can rapidly reverse deep/profound blockade (even after high-dose rocuronium, within 2–3 min).
  • Neostigmine requires spontaneous recovery to at least moderate block (TOF count ≥2) before being effective.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Neostigmine reverses rocuronium by direct encapsulation, while sugammadex works by acetylcholinesterase inhibition: Incorrect.

 

  • Neostigmine: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → ↑ ACh at NMJ → competes with NDMR.
  • Sugammadex: Modified γ-cyclodextrin → directly encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium in plasma → rapid reversal.
  •  The mechanisms are reversed in this statement.

 

Option C. Neostigmine is safer in patients with severe bradycardia, whereas sugammadex requires co-administration of atropine or glycopyrrolate: Incorrect.

 

  • Neostigmine: Can cause bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions, hence always given with anticholinergic (glycopyrrolate or atropine).
  • Sugammadex: No need for anticholinergic; safer in bradycardic patients.

 

Option D. Both sugammadex and neostigmine are equally effective against benzylisoquinolinium agents like atracurium: Incorrect.

 

  • Sugammadex is specific for aminosteroid NDMRs (rocuronium, vecuronium).
  • It is ineffective against benzylisoquinoliniums (atracurium, cisatracurium). Neostigmine works on all NDMRs (though slower).

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is started on hormonal therapy. The oncologist considers whether to use a GnRH agonist (like leuprolide) or a GnRH antagonist (like degarelix). Which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both GnRH agonists and antagonists initially cause a testosterone “flare” before suppression

options.label: B
options.text: GnRH agonists downregulate pituitary GnRH receptors after continuous administration, while antagonists directly block them

options.label: C
options.text: GnRH antagonists are less effective than agonists in achieving castrate testosterone levels

options.label: D
options.text: Both classes are contraindicated in endometriosis because they worsen estrogen effects

questions.answerText: GnRH agonists downregulate pituitary GnRH receptors after continuous administration, while antagonists directly block them
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) GnRH agonists downregulate pituitary GnRH receptors after continuous administration, while antagonists directly block them

 

  • Agonists: Continuous use → receptor desensitization/downregulation.
  • Antagonists: Competitive blockade at pituitary GnRH receptors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Both GnRH agonists and antagonists initially cause a testosterone “flare” before suppression: Incorrect.

 

  • GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin): Initially stimulate GnRH receptor → transient LH/FSH surge = testosterone flare → later downregulation & suppression.
  • GnRH antagonists (degarelix, cetrorelix, ganirelix): Directly block receptors → no flare.

 

Option C. GnRH antagonists are less effective than agonists in achieving castrate testosterone levels: Incorrect. Both achieve medical castration levels. In fact, antagonists act faster and avoid flare.

 

Option D. Both classes are contraindicated in endometriosis because they worsen estrogen effects: Incorrect. Both agonists & antagonists are actually used to treat endometriosis (by suppressing estrogen). They don’t worsen estrogen effects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin): Cause flare → suppression.
  • GnRH antagonists (degarelix, cetrorelix, ganirelix): Cause immediate suppression, no flare.
  • Both are used in prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, assisted reproduction protocols.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes. The child had fever (39°C) for 1 day due to an upper respiratory infection. He returns to baseline within 10 minutes, has a normal neurological exam, and no signs of meningitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Start daily valproate prophylaxis to prevent future febrile seizures

options.label: B
options.text: Give oral diazepam prophylaxis during future febrile illnesses

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure parents; no long-term anticonvulsant therapy is required

options.label: D
options.text: Perform immediate lumbar puncture and start IV acyclovir

questions.answerText: Reassure parents; no long-term anticonvulsant therapy is required
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Reassure parents; no long-term anticonvulsant therapy is required

 

Simple febrile seizure = generalized, <15 min, occurs once in 24h, neurologically normal child. Best management = reassurance, fever control (antipyretics), and parental education. No long-term drugs needed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Start daily valproate prophylaxis to prevent future febrile seizures: False. Continuous antiepileptics (valproate, phenobarbital) are not recommended for simple febrile seizures due to adverse effects outweighing benefits.

 

Option B. Give oral diazepam prophylaxis during future febrile illnesses: (PARTLY TRUE but not first choice here). Intermittent diazepam prophylaxis (oral or rectal) during febrile illness can reduce recurrence, but is only considered in recurrent or complex febrile seizures. Not indicated after a single simple febrile seizure.

 

Option D. Perform immediate lumbar puncture and start IV acyclovir: False. Reserved if there are meningitis/encephalitis features (neck stiffness, altered sensorium, prolonged seizure, bulging fontanelle). Not needed here since child is well and neurologically normal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Simple febrile seizure: Generalized, <15 min, no recurrence in 24h, normal neuro exam → no long-term therapy.
  • Complex febrile seizure: Focal, >15 min, or recurrent in 24h → may need further evaluation.
  • Prophylaxis: Continuous AEDs not recommended; intermittent diazepam during febrile illness sometimes used in high-risk/recurrent cases.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Burkitt lymphoma develops tumor lysis syndrome after initiation of chemotherapy. His serum uric acid is markedly elevated. He is given rasburicase, which rapidly lowers uric acid and prevents renal damage. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of rasburicase?

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrolysis of uric acid into allantoin by recombinant uricase

options.label: B
options.text: Activation of the uricase enzyme, facilitating uric acid breakdown

options.label: C
options.text: Oxidation of uric acid into allantoin and hydrogen peroxide by recombinant urate oxidase

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibition of xanthine oxidase, preventing formation of uric acid

questions.answerText: Oxidation of uric acid into allantoin and hydrogen peroxide by recombinant urate oxidase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Oxidation of uric acid into allantoin and hydrogen peroxide by recombinant urate oxidase

 

  • Rasburicase = recombinant uricase → converts uric acid → allantoin + H₂O₂.
    • Allantoin = highly water-soluble, excreted easily.
    • Works rapidly → ideal for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS).
    • Produces hydrogen peroxide → contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolysis, methemoglobinemia).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydrolysis of uric acid into allantoin by recombinant uricase: Incorrect. Rasburicase does not hydrolyze uric acid; it specifically catalyzes an oxidation reaction.

 

Option B. Activation of the uricase enzyme, facilitating uric acid breakdown: Incorrect. Humans naturally lack uricase, so there is nothing to “activate.” Rasburicase is a recombinant form of uricase, not an activator.

 

Option D. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase, preventing formation of uric acid: Incorrect. That’s the mechanism of allopurinol, febuxostat, which prevent new uric acid formation but don’t clear existing uric acid.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with long-standing diabetic gastroparesis presents with nausea, bloating, and early satiety. He is started on a drug that improves gastric emptying by enhancing ACh release in the GI tract, and also acts as an antiemetic via D₂ receptor blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). Two weeks later, he develops restlessness, involuntary facial grimacing, and galactorrhea. Which of the following statements about this drug is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It acts as a muscarinic agonist in the gut and causes diarrhea as its main side effect

options.label: B
options.text: It blocks both D₂ receptors in CTZ and 5-HT₃ receptors in the gut, while agonizing 5-HT₄ receptors

options.label: C
options.text: It is contraindicated in patients with GERD due to decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone

options.label: D
options.text: It increases prolactin by blocking dopamine D₁ receptors in the pituitary

questions.answerText: It blocks both D₂ receptors in CTZ and 5-HT₃ receptors in the gut, while agonizing 5-HT₄ receptors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It blocks both D₂ receptors in CTZ and 5-HT₃ receptors in the gut, while agonizing 5-HT₄ receptors

 

  • D₂ receptor blockade (CTZ): Antiemetic effect
  • 5-HT₃ receptor blockade (gut): Antiemetic effect
  • 5-HT₄ receptor agonism: Prokinetic effect (↑ gastric emptying, ↑ LES tone)
    → Explains both clinical uses & side effects.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It acts as a muscarinic agonist in the gut and causes diarrhea as its main side effect: Incorrect. Metoclopramide is not a muscarinic agonist. It indirectly ↑ ACh release in the GI tract by blocking presynaptic D₂ receptors. Diarrhea can occur but is not the main side effect.

 

Option C. It is contraindicated in patients with GERD due to decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone: Incorrect. Actually the opposite: metoclopramide increases LES tone → useful in GERD & gastroparesis.

 

Option D. It increases prolactin by blocking dopamine D₁ receptors in the pituitary: Incorrect. Hyperprolactinemia occurs because of D₂ blockade in the pituitary, not D₁.

 

Educational Objective:

 

(Metoclopramide):

 

  • Mechanism:
    • D₂ antagonist (CTZ) → antiemetic
    • 5-HT₃ antagonist (gut) + 5-HT₄ agonist → prokinetic
  • Uses: Gastroparesis (esp. diabetic), GERD, antiemetic in chemo/post-op.
  • Adverse effects: EPS (dystonia, Parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), akathisia, hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, gynecomastia, amenorrhea).
  • Contraindications: Parkinson’s disease, small bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is not used for chemoprophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Azithromycin

 

Not recommended for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rifampicin: Standard prophylaxis (600 mg PO q12h × 2 days in adults).

 

Option B. Ciprofloxacin: Single oral dose alternative in adults.

 

Option C. Ceftriaxone: Single IM injection, especially in pregnancy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Only Rifampicin, Ciprofloxacin, Ceftriaxone are approved.
  • Azithromycin may sometimes reduce nasopharyngeal carriage, but it is not standard prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ER with sudden-onset palpitations. ECG shows narrow QRS tachycardia (PSVT) at 180/min. She is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following cannot terminate an acute attack of PSVT?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Intravenous Digoxin

 

Digoxin works by increasing vagal tone, but its onset is too slow to terminate acute PSVT. It is only useful for prophylaxis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Carotid sinus massage: Effective. A vagal maneuver → ↑ vagal tone → slows AV nodal conduction → may terminate PSVT.

 

Option B. Intravenous adenosine: Effective. Drug of choice for acute PSVT termination. Very rapid onset and short half-life.

 

Option C. Intravenous Verapamil: Effective. Calcium channel blocker (non-DHP) → slows AV nodal conduction → used if adenosine is contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with HIV infection (CD4 count 40/µL) is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. He is started on both ART and ATT on the same day. After 2 weeks, he presents with high fever, worsening cough, and enlarging cervical lymph nodes despite good adherence to therapy. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this paradoxical worsening?

options.label: B
options.text: ART-induced hepatotoxicity leading to poor ATT absorption

options.label: D
options.text: Drug–drug interaction between rifampicin and protease inhibitors reducing ATT efficacy

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)

 

  • Occurs when ART is started early (simultaneous with ATT or within first 2 weeks) in patients with CD4 <50.
  • Restored immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against TB antigens → clinical worsening despite effective therapy.
  • Management: Continue both ATT + ART; add corticosteroids if severe.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: Incorrect. Resistance usually presents as failure to improve microbiologically, not sudden inflammatory worsening after ART initiation.

 

Option B. ART-induced hepatotoxicity leading to poor ATT absorption: Incorrect. Would cause jaundice, hepatomegaly, LFT elevation, not worsening TB symptoms.

 

Option D. Drug–drug interaction between rifampicin and protease inhibitors reducing ATT efficacy: Incorrect. This interaction causes low ART efficacy, leading to HIV progression, not paradoxical TB worsening.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the BPaL regimen is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It combines Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, and Levofloxacin for 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole derivative that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and releases nitric oxide under anaerobic conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Bedaquiline in this regimen acts by inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall

options.label: D
options.text: This regimen is only used in drug-susceptible pulmonary TB as first-line therapy

questions.answerText: Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole derivative that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and releases nitric oxide under anaerobic conditions
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole derivative that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and releases nitric oxide under anaerobic conditions

 

  • Pretomanid = a nitroimidazo-oxazine derivative.
    • In aerobic bacilli → inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (cell wall).
    • In anaerobic/dormant bacilli → releases nitric oxide, killing latent organisms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It combines Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, and Levofloxacin for 6 months: Incorrect. BPaL regimen = Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid, not levofloxacin.

 

Option C. Bedaquiline in this regimen acts by inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall: Incorrect. Bedaquiline acts by inhibiting mycobacterial ATP synthase, not mycolic acid synthesis.

 

Option D. This regimen is only used in drug-susceptible pulmonary TB as first-line therapy: Incorrect. BPaL is not for drug-susceptible TB. It is specifically for XDR-TB or MDR-TB resistant to fluoroquinolones.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the effect of Class I antiarrhythmic subgroups on the ventricular action potential?

options.label: A
options.text: Class Ia drugs prolong phase 0 depolarization and increase action potential duration (APD) by blocking Na⁺ and some K⁺ channels

options.label: B
options.text: Class Ib drugs strongly depress phase 0 depolarization and markedly prolong action potential duration

options.label: C
options.text: Class Ic drugs mildly depress phase 0 depolarization and shorten action potential duration in ischemic tissue

options.label: D
options.text: All Class I drugs produce the same effect on action potential duration but differ only in their potency of Na⁺ channel block

questions.answerText: Class Ia drugs prolong phase 0 depolarization and increase action potential duration (APD) by blocking Na⁺ and some K⁺ channels
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Class Ia drugs prolong phase 0 depolarization and increase action potential duration (APD) by blocking Na⁺ and some K⁺ channels

 

  • Drugs: Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide
  • Block Na⁺ channels (phase 0) → slow conduction velocity
  • Also block some K⁺ channels (phase 3) → ↑ APD & ↑ ERP → QT prolongation

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Class Ib drugs strongly depress phase 0 depolarization and markedly prolong action potential duration: Incorrect.

 

  • Drugs: Lidocaine, Mexiletine, Phenytoin
  • Cause weak Na⁺ block, minimal effect on phase 0 in normal tissue
  • Shorten APD & ERP (due to effect on late Na⁺ current)
  • Especially effective in ischemic myocardium
  • So they do not markedly prolong APD (opposite effect).

 

Option C. Class Ic drugs mildly depress phase 0 depolarization and shorten action potential duration in ischemic tissue: Incorrect.

 

  • Drugs: Flecainide, Propafenone
  • Cause strong Na⁺ block, markedly slow phase 0 upstroke → ↓ conduction velocity
  • Little/no effect on APD or ERP
  • They do not shorten APD significantly.

 

Option D. All Class I drugs produce the same effect on action potential duration but differ only in their potency of Na⁺ channel block: Incorrect.

 

  • Class I subclasses differ both in strength of Na⁺ block and effect on AP duration:
    • Ia = ↑ APD
    • Ib = ↓ APD
    • Ic = ↔ APD

 

Summary Table — Class I drugs vs Action Potential

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on haloperidol. After 5 days, he develops stiffness, mask-like face, tremors, and rigidity. On examination, cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia are present. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his current condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Add benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl) or benztropine

 

These are centrally acting anticholinergics used to treat drug-induced Parkinsonism & acute dystonia (EPS due to dopamine blockade).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Taper haloperidol and add propranolol: Incorrect. Propranolol is used for akathisia (inner restlessness, pacing, inability to sit still), not for drug-induced Parkinsonism.

 

Option C. Add lorazepam for sedation: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines can help in akathisia or acute agitation, but not the best treatment for Parkinsonian EPS.

 

Option D. Give levodopa-carbidopa combination: Incorrect. Not used for antipsychotic-induced Parkinsonism, because it may worsen psychosis.

 

High-Yield EPS & Treatment

questions.stem: An HIV-positive pregnant woman presents in the third trimester with viral load 1200 copies/mL and is started immediately on ART. She delivers vaginally at 38 weeks and the baby is kept on exclusive breastfeeding. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis for the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Nevirapine single dose and continue breast feeding

options.label: B
options.text: Nevirapine for 6 weeks and continue breast feeding

options.label: C
options.text: Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 6 weeks and continue formula feeding

options.label: D
options.text: Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding

questions.answerText: Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding

 

  • Mother was not on effective ART before delivery (late start, high VL >1000).
  • Baby is breastfed → High-risk infant → needs dual prophylaxis (ZDV + NVP) for 12 weeks.
  • If formula-fed instead → only 6 weeks dual prophylaxis would be enough.
  • If mother had been on effective ART and VL suppressed → Nevirapine 6 weeks only, regardless of feeding choice.

 

Neonatal HIV Prophylaxis Table (per WHO/NACO)

questions.stem: A patient undergoing surgery is administered a neuromuscular blocking agent for muscle relaxation during induction of anesthesia. Shortly after administration, the patient develops flushing, hypotension, and bronchospasm. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this reaction?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Atracurium

 

  • A benzylisoquinolinium NDMR.
  • Known for histamine release, causing flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm.
  • It undergoes Hofmann elimination (organ-independent metabolism).
  • Side effect: laudanosine metabolite → seizures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vecuronium: Incorrect.

 

  • Steroidal NDMR.
  • Does not cause histamine release. Cardiovascularly stable.

 

Option C. Cisatracurium: Incorrect.

 

  • A stereoisomer of atracurium, but does not release histamine significantly.
  • Also undergoes Hofmann elimination, preferred in renal/hepatic dysfunction.

 

Option D. Pancuronium: Incorrect.

 

  • Steroidal NDMR.
  • No histamine release.
  • Side effect: tachycardia, hypertension (due to vagolytic + sympathetic stimulation).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF 35%) is being evaluated for optimization of therapy. His HbA1c is 7.8% despite metformin. Renal function: eGFR = 35 mL/min/1.73 m². The physician considers starting an SGLT2 inhibitor. Which of the following statements regarding this drug class is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: They improve glycemic control by increasing insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells

options.label: B
options.text: They reduce preload and afterload in heart failure by promoting osmotic diuresis and natriuresis

options.label: C
options.text: They increase the risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy

options.label: D
options.text: They are contraindicated in patients with diabetic nephropathy because of nephrotoxicity

questions.answerText: They reduce preload and afterload in heart failure by promoting osmotic diuresis and natriuresis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) They reduce preload and afterload in heart failure by promoting osmotic diuresis and natriuresis


SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) cause osmotic diuresis + natriuresis, which reduces preload (volume load) and afterload (BP).
→ Proven to improve outcomes in HFrEF and CKD, even in non-diabetics.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. They improve glycemic control by increasing insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells: Incorrect. SGLT2 inhibitors act in the proximal tubule of the kidney by blocking glucose reabsorption, causing glycosuria. They do not increase insulin secretion (that’s sulfonylureas, meglitinides).

 

Option C. They increase the risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy: Incorrect. They do not cause hypoglycemia when used alone, since mechanism is insulin-independent. Hypoglycemia risk arises only when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.

 

Option D. They are contraindicated in patients with diabetic nephropathy because of nephrotoxicity: Incorrect. Far from nephrotoxic — they are actually renoprotective (reduce intraglomerular pressure, slow CKD progression). They are used down to eGFR ~20–25 mL/min (depending on drug).
