questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with onychomycosis involving 2 toenails. He has mild liver disease and wants to avoid systemic antifungals. The dermatologist prescribes a topical antifungal nail lacquer. Which of the following drugs is most likely prescribed?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Amorolfine

 

  • A topical antifungal nail lacquer (5%), applied 1–2 times weekly.
  • Inhibits ergosterol synthesis (Δ14 reductase and Δ7–Δ8 isomerase inhibition).
  • Used for onychomycosis when ≤3 nails involved or systemic therapy contraindicated (e.g., liver disease).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Griseofulvin: Incorrect.

 

  • Oral antifungal, binds to microtubules and keratin.
  • Not available as nail lacquer, and avoided in liver disease.

 

Option C. Nystatin: Incorrect.

 

  • Polyene antifungal, used topically for Candida (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis).
  • Not effective in onychomycosis, not available as lacquer.

 

Option D. Itraconazole: Incorrect.

 

  • Oral triazole antifungal used for onychomycosis (pulse therapy).
  • Contraindicated in liver disease and not available as lacquer.

questions.stem: Which of the following antidote–poison pairs is correctly matched?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hydroxocobalamin – Cyanide poisoning

 

  • Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide → forms cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) → safely excreted.
  • Alternative antidotes: Sodium thiosulfate, Sodium nitrite, Dicobalt edetate.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Flumazenil – Opioid overdose: Incorrect.

  • Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist, not for opioids.
  • Naloxone is the antidote for opioid overdose.

 

Option C. Fomepizole – Organophosphate poisoning: Incorrect.

 

  • Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase → antidote for methanol & ethylene glycol poisoning.
  • Organophosphate antidotes = Atropine + Pralidoxime.

 

Option D. Deferoxamine – Lead poisoning: Incorrect.
 

  • Deferoxamine chelates iron (Fe³⁺).
  • Lead poisoning antidotes = EDTA, Dimercaprol, DMSA (succimer).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer is started on a targeted drug in combination with endocrine therapy. The drug inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK 4/6), thereby blocking phosphorylation of Rb protein and halting the cell cycle at the G1 → S checkpoint. Which of the following drugs acts by this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Palbociclib

 

  • CDK 4/6 inhibitor.
  • Blocks Rb phosphorylation → prevents E2F release → arrests cell cycle at G1 phase.
  • Used in HR+ HER2− breast cancer, often with letrozole/fulvestrant.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Imatinib: Incorrect.

 

  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BCR-ABL, c-KIT, PDGFR).
  • Used in CML, GIST.

 

Option C. Olaparib: Incorrect.

 

  • PARP inhibitor → causes accumulation of DNA damage.
  • Used in BRCA-mutated ovarian/breast cancers.

 

Option D. Bevacizumab: Incorrect.

 

  • Monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A.
  • Anti-angiogenic, used in colorectal cancer, RCC, glioblastoma, etc.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Tofacitinib is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used in rheumatoid arthritis

options.label: B
options.text: It is administered by intravenous route

options.label: C
options.text: It carries a black box warning of increased risk of infections

options.label: D
options.text: It has been associated with increased risk of herpes zoster reactivation

questions.answerText: It is administered by intravenous route
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It is administered by intravenous route

 

Tofacitinib is not IV; it is an oral small molecule (a key difference from biologics like TNF inhibitors which are injectables).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used in rheumatoid arthritis: True. Tofacitinib = oral JAK inhibitor (mainly JAK1 & JAK3). Used in RA, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis.

 

Option C. It carries a black box warning of increased risk of infections: True. Carries an FDA black box warning for serious infections, malignancy, thrombosis. Opportunistic infections (e.g., TB, fungal, viral) can occur.

 

Option D. It has been associated with increased risk of herpes zoster reactivation: True. Associated with increased risk of herpes zoster reactivation (higher than TNF-α inhibitors).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male patient presents with hypertension. His medical history reveals bilateral renal artery stenosis. Which of the following antihypertensive medications is absolutely contraindicated in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Captopril

 

ACE inhibitors like captopril are absolutely contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis. In this condition, both kidneys depend on angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction of efferent arterioles to maintain glomerular filtration pressure. ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation, leading to loss of this compensatory mechanism. This results in severe reduction in glomerular filtration rate, potentially causing acute renal failure. The mechanism involves loss of preferential efferent arteriolar constriction that normally maintains filtration pressure across stenotic renal arteries.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Amlodipine: This calcium channel blocker is safe in bilateral renal artery stenosis as it does not interfere with the renin-angiotensin system and may actually improve renal blood flow through vasodilation. 

 

Option B.  Propranolol: Beta blockers can be used cautiously in renal artery stenosis. While they may reduce renin release, they do not directly compromise the angiotensin II-dependent filtration mechanism. 

 

Option D. Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide diuretics can be used in renal artery stenosis, though they may cause some reduction in GFR, they do not have the severe contraindication that ACE inhibitors have.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis because they eliminate angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, which is essential for maintaining GFR in stenotic kidneys.

questions.stem: According to the pharmacokinetic properties of corticosteroids, which statement correctly describes the relative activities of different steroids?

options.label: A
options.text: Cortisone has the maximum glucocorticoid activity

options.label: B
options.text: Dexamethasone has maximum glucocorticoid activity with zero mineralocorticoid activity

questions.answerText: Dexamethasone has maximum glucocorticoid activity with zero mineralocorticoid activity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dexamethasone has maximum glucocorticoid activity with zero mineralocorticoid activity

 

According to the steroid potency chart, dexamethasone has maximum glucocorticoid activity (relative potency = 30) with zero mineralocorticoid activity, making it ideal for conditions requiring pure anti-inflammatory effects without sodium retention. The equivalent dose is 0.75 mg, making it highly potent. Betamethasone is actually the most potent glucocorticoid (potency = 25) but dexamethasone has maximum activity. Dexamethasone's long duration of action and selective glucocorticoid activity make it useful in conditions like cerebral edema and inflammatory disorders where mineralocorticoid effects are undesirable.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Cortisone has the maximum glucocorticoid activity: Incorrect. Cortisone has minimum glucocorticoid activity (0.8) and is the least potent glucocorticoid with equivalent dose of 25 mg.

 

Option C. Hydrocortisone has maximum mineralocorticoid activity: Wrong. Aldosterone has maximum mineralocorticoid activity (3000), though it's not used clinically. Among clinically used drugs, fludrocortisone has maximum mineralocorticoid activity (250). 

 

Option D. Fludrocortisone has maximum glucocorticoid activity: Incorrect. Fludrocortisone has maximum mineralocorticoid activity among clinically used drugs, with moderate glucocorticoid activity (10).

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Dexamethasone has maximum glucocorticoid activity with zero mineralocorticoid activity, making it ideal for anti-inflammatory therapy without electrolyte disturbances.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with continuous seizure activity lasting more than 30 minutes. The records of the patient show that he has GTCS 2 times in last one month. Which is the most appropriate drug that should be used to treat this person now?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lorazepam

 

Lorazepam is the drug of choice for status epilepticus because it provides rapid onset of action when given intravenously and has a longer duration of action compared to diazepam. Lorazepam acts by enhancing GABA-mediated chloride channel opening, increasing the frequency of channel opening and providing powerful anticonvulsant effects. Its longer half-life in the brain (compared to diazepam) makes it more suitable for sustained seizure control. The drug can be given intravenously for immediate effect or rectally when IV access is not available.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Valproate: While valproate is drug of choice for treatment of GTCS, it is not the answer here. As the question is being asked about management of status epilepticus, so first choice is lorazepam. 

 

Option C. Carbamazepine: This drug is not suitable for status epilepticus as it cannot be given intravenously and has slower onset of action. 

 

Option D. Ethosuximide: It is first line drug for treatment of absence seizures along with valproate. It has no role in status epilepticus.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Lorazepam is the drug of choice for status epilepticus due to its rapid onset, IV compatibility, and longer brain half-life compared to other benzodiazepines.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient with bronchial asthma is prescribed zafirlukast for long-term control. This medication improves her condition by targeting which of the following mechanisms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Blocks leukotriene receptors

 

Zafirlukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist that blocks the effects of leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 at their receptors in the airways. Leukotrienes are potent inflammatory mediators that cause bronchoconstriction, increased mucus secretion, and airway inflammation in asthma. By blocking leukotriene receptors, zafirlukast prevents these inflammatory responses and provides anti-inflammatory effects. It is administered orally and is effective in reducing the frequency of asthma attacks, particularly in aspirin-sensitive asthma and exercise-induced bronchospasm.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Inhibits 5-lipoxygenase enzyme: This is the mechanism of zileuton, which prevents leukotriene synthesis rather than blocking their receptors. 

 

Option C. Activates β2-adrenergic receptors: This is the mechanism of bronchodilators like salbutamol and terbutaline, not zafirlukast. 

 

Option D. Inhibits phosphodiesterase-4: This is the mechanism of theophylline and specific PDE4 inhibitors, not leukotriene receptor antagonists.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Zafirlukast blocks leukotriene receptors to prevent leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and inflammation, providing prophylactic anti-asthmatic effects.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is on long-term warfarin therapy. He develops a urinary tract infection and is prescribed a sulfonamide antibiotic. A few days later, he presents with gum bleeding and multiple ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show an elevated INR. This drug–drug interaction is most likely explained by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: B
options.text: Sulfonamides displace warfarin from albumin binding sites

questions.answerText: Sulfonamides displace warfarin from albumin binding sites
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sulfonamides displace warfarin from albumin binding sites

 

Warfarin is highly bound to plasma albumin (>95%), and only the free (unbound) fraction is pharmacologically active. Sulfonamides compete with warfarin for the same albumin binding sites and displace warfarin from these sites. This displacement increases the free warfarin concentration, leading to enhanced anticoagulant effects and potential bleeding complications. This is a classic example of plasma protein binding displacement interaction where displacement of highly protein-bound drugs can lead to increased toxicity due to higher free drug concentrations.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Sulfonamides inhibit warfarin metabolism: Incorrect. Sulfonamides do not significantly affect warfarin metabolism; the interaction is purely due to protein binding displacement.

 

Option C. Sulfonamides enhance warfarin absorption: Incorrect. The interaction occurs at the level of protein binding in plasma, not during absorption from the GI tract. 

 

Option D. Sulfonamides inhibit warfarin excretion: Incorrect. Warfarin is primarily metabolized by the liver, not excreted unchanged, and sulfonamides don't affect its elimination significantly.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Sulfonamides displace warfarin from albumin binding sites, increasing free warfarin concentration and enhancing anticoagulant effects, demonstrating the clinical significance of protein binding displacement interactions.

questions.stem: In drug development, Phase Zero studies are conducted in humans with what primary objective?

options.label: B
options.text: To know the pharmacokinetics of the drug

options.label: C
options.text: To establish efficacy in large populations

questions.answerText: To know the pharmacokinetics of the drug
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) To know the pharmacokinetics of the drug

 

Phase Zero studies are micro-dosing studies conducted in humans using very small amounts of the investigational drug (maximum 100 mcg or 1/100th of Human Equivalent Dose, whichever is lower). The primary objective is to understand the pharmacokinetics of the drug in humans, including absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion patterns. Radiolabeled substances are often used to track the drug's behavior. These studies cannot determine efficacy or safety but provide valuable pharmacokinetic data that helps in planning subsequent Phase I studies.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. To determine maximum tolerated dose: This is the objective of Phase I studies, not Phase Zero studies, which use sub-therapeutic micro-doses. 

 

Option C. To establish efficacy in large populations: This is the objective of Phase III studies involving large patient populations for efficacy confirmation. 

 

Option D. To identify rare side effects: This is part of Phase IV post-marketing surveillance studies, not Phase Zero micro-dosing studies.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Phase Zero studies use micro-dosing in humans to determine pharmacokinetic properties of investigational drugs before proceeding to Phase I dose-escalation studies.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with streptococcal pharyngitis and is prescribed oral penicillin V. This drug kills bacteria by interfering with which of the following processes in bacterial cell wall synthesis?

options.label: B
options.text: Chain elongation formed by basic units of peptidoglycan

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Peptidoglycan cross-linking

 

Penicillin exerts its bactericidal effect by inhibiting the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls. Penicillin binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), particularly transpeptidases, which are responsible for forming cross-links between peptidoglycan chains. This inhibition results in a weakened cell wall that cannot withstand osmotic pressure, leading to bacterial lysis and death. The mechanism is specific to bacterial cells since human cells lack cell walls and peptidoglycan synthesis machinery, explaining penicillin's selective toxicity.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option B. Chain elongation formed by basic units of peptidoglycan: This is the target of vancomycin. 

 

Option C. Protein synthesis: This is inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides, not by penicillin

 

Option D. RNA transcription: This is the target of rifampin and some antiviral drugs, not penicillin's mechanism of action.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Penicillin kills bacteria by inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking in cell wall synthesis, leading to osmotic lysis due to weakened cell walls.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man is hospitalized with a large, purulent abscess on his forearm. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to oxacillin, nafcillin, and methicillin. Which of the following best explains this bacterial resistance pattern?

options.label: B
options.text: Formation of alternative penicillin-binding proteins with reduced affinity

questions.answerText: Formation of alternative penicillin-binding proteins with reduced affinity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Formation of alternative penicillin-binding proteins with reduced affinity

 

MRSA develops resistance through the formation of alternative penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that have markedly reduced affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics. The mecA gene encodes for PBP2a (also called PBP2'), which has very low affinity for all beta-lactam antibiotics including methicillin, penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems. This alternative PBP can carry out transpeptidase function for cell wall synthesis even in the presence of beta-lactam antibiotics. Since this resistance mechanism affects the target site rather than drug inactivation, MRSA is resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics, making vancomycin or teicoplanin the drugs of choice.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Production of extended-spectrum beta-lactamases: This is a mechanism of resistance seen in gram-negative bacteria, not the primary mechanism in MRSA resistance. 

 

Option C. Development of efflux pumps: This mechanism is important for resistance to drugs like tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones, but not the primary mechanism for MRSA beta-lactam resistance. 

 

Option D. Alteration of cell wall permeability: This mechanism affects drug penetration but is not the primary mechanism for MRSA resistance to beta-lactams.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

MRSA resistance occurs due to alternative PBPs (PBP2a) with reduced affinity for beta-lactams, making all beta-lactam antibiotics ineffective and requiring vancomycin or teicoplanin therapy.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic kidney disease presents with muscle weakness and palpitations. ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. As part of acute management, he is given a medication via inhalation that lowers serum potassium by promoting its shift into cells. Which of the following agents was most likely administered?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Salbutamol

 

Inhaled salbutamol is an effective emergency treatment for hyperkalemia because it promotes cellular uptake of potassium through β2-adrenergic receptor activation. The mechanism involves stimulation of Na+/K+-ATPase pump, which shifts potassium from extracellular to intracellular compartments, rapidly lowering serum potassium levels. Salbutamol can be given intravenously or by inhalation, with the inhalational route being safer and equally effective. This treatment provides rapid onset (within 30 minutes) and can lower serum potassium by 0.5-1.0 mEq/L.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Calcium gluconate: While used in hyperkalemia emergencies, calcium gluconate stabilizes cardiac membranes and antagonizes cardiac conduction abnormalities rather than shifting potassium into cells. 

 

Option B. Sodium bicarbonate: This does shift potassium into cells by alkalinizing blood, but it cannot be given by inhalation route and is less preferred due to potential complications.

 

Option D. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate: This resin binds potassium in the gut for elimination but does not shift potassium into cells and is used for non-emergency treatment.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Inhaled salbutamol treats hyperkalemia emergency by promoting cellular potassium uptake through β2-receptor stimulation and Na+/K+-ATPase activation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a urinary tract infection is treated with an aminoglycoside antibiotic. Even after the drug concentration in his plasma drops below the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the bacterial growth remains suppressed for several hours. Which of the following terms best describes this phenomenon?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Post-antibiotic effect

 

The post-antibiotic effect (PAE) refers to the persistent suppression of bacterial growth after a short exposure to an antimicrobial agent, even when drug concentrations fall below the MIC.

 

  • This effect occurs because the antibiotic causes prolonged disruption of bacterial physiology—such as persistent inhibition of protein or nucleic acid synthesis—despite the absence of detectable drug levels.
  • PAE is seen with several antibiotic classes, including aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and certain beta-lactams.
  • Clinically, PAE allows for extended dosing intervals without loss of efficacy, which can reduce toxicity and improve patient compliance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Sequential blockade: This is the combined use of two drugs that inhibit sequential steps in a metabolic pathway (e.g., trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole in folate synthesis). It is unrelated to the persistent effect after drug removal.

 

Option C. Concentration-dependent killing: Refers to antibiotics (e.g., aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) whose efficacy increases with higher peak drug concentrations. While aminoglycosides exhibit both concentration-dependent killing and PAE, the phenomenon described in the question specifically matches PAE.

 

Option D. Time-dependent killing: Refers to antibiotics (e.g., beta-lactams, vancomycin) whose efficacy depends on the duration that the drug concentration remains above the MIC, not on persistence after levels drop below the MIC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The post-antibiotic effect is the persistent suppression of bacterial growth after limited antibiotic exposure, even when plasma drug levels fall below the minimum inhibitory concentration.

questions.stem: In immunocompromised patients such as those with neutropenia, bactericidal antibiotics are preferred over bacteriostatic antibiotics. Which of the following is a bactericidal antibiotic?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ciprofloxacin

 

Ciprofloxacin is a bactericidal fluoroquinolone antibiotic that kills bacteria by inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, essential enzymes for DNA replication and repair. Bactericidal antibiotics are preferred in immunocompromised patients because they directly kill bacteria rather than just inhibiting their growth. In neutropenic patients, the immune system cannot effectively clear bacteria that are merely growth-inhibited, making bactericidal activity crucial for clinical success. Fluoroquinolones demonstrate concentration-dependent killing and significant post-antibiotic effects.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Chloramphenicol: This is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that inhibits protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit, only inhibiting bacterial growth rather than killing bacteria. 

 

Option B. Tetracycline: This is also bacteriostatic, working by inhibiting protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing bacterial growth but not directly killing bacteria. 

 

Option C. Erythromycin: This macrolide antibiotic is bacteriostatic, inhibiting protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Bactericidal antibiotics like fluoroquinolones are preferred in immunocompromised patients because they kill bacteria directly rather than relying on host immune system to clear growth-inhibited organisms.

questions.stem: According to the classification of adverse drug reactions, which example best represents a Type B adverse drug reaction?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Allergic reaction to penicillin

 

Type B (Bizarre) adverse drug reactions are unpredictable, not dose-related, and occur in susceptible individuals regardless of dose. Allergic reactions to penicillin exemplify Type B reactions because they are immunologically mediated, can occur with minimal doses, cannot be predicted from the drug's pharmacology, and occur only in sensitized individuals. These reactions involve hypersensitivity mechanisms and can range from mild skin rashes to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Type B reactions are contrasted with Type A (Augmented) reactions, which are predictable, dose-related extensions of the drug's pharmacological effects.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Dose-related hepatotoxicity with paracetamol: This is a Type A reaction because it's predictable, dose-related, and represents an extension of the drug's metabolic pathway leading to toxic metabolite formation. 

 

Option C. Osteoporosis with prednisolone: This is a Type C reaction as it occurs only on chronic use of steroids. 

 

Option D. Rebound hypertension on clonidine withdrawal: This is a Type E reaction because occurs when a drug is suddenly withdrawan (End of dose) 

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Type B adverse drug reactions are unpredictable, immunologically mediated responses (like penicillin allergy) that are not dose-related and occur only in susceptible individuals.

questions.stem: Despite having short half-lives (0.5-2 hours), proton pump inhibitors can suppress acid secretion for more than 24 hours. What accounts for this prolonged duration of action?

options.label: A
options.text: They are available as sustained-release formulations

options.label: C
options.text: They irreversibly inhibit the proton pump molecule

options.label: D
options.text: They have active metabolites with longer half-lives

questions.answerText: They irreversibly inhibit the proton pump molecule
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) They irreversibly inhibit the proton pump molecule

 

Proton pump inhibitors are prodrugs that become activated in the acidic environment of parietal cell canaliculi, forming sulfenamide which binds covalently to sulfhydryl groups of cysteine residues in H+/K+-ATPase. This irreversible binding permanently inactivates the pump molecule, and acid secretion can only resume after new pump molecules are synthesized and inserted into the membrane. This "hit and run" mechanism explains why PPIs have prolonged effects (24-48 hours) despite short plasma half-lives. The irreversible nature distinguishes PPIs from H2 blockers, which are competitive reversible inhibitors.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. They are available as sustained-release formulations: While PPIs are enteric-coated to prevent acid degradation, this doesn't explain the prolonged duration beyond the coating's purpose. 

 

Option B. They undergo extensive enterohepatic circulation: PPIs do not have significant enterohepatic circulation that would explain their prolonged effect.

 

Option D. They have active metabolites with longer half-lives: PPI metabolites are inactive; the prolonged effect is due to irreversible enzyme inhibition, not active metabolites.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

PPIs have prolonged duration of action (24-48 hours) despite short half-lives because they irreversibly inhibit H+/K+-ATPase, requiring new enzyme synthesis for acid secretion recovery.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is diagnosed with a duodenal ulcer and is prescribed ranitidine and sucralfate. Despite adherence, his symptoms persist. Which of the following best explains why this drug combination is considered irrational?

options.label: C
options.text: Ranitidine raises gastric pH, preventing sucralfate polymerization

options.label: D
options.text: The combination causes severe drug interactions

questions.answerText: Ranitidine raises gastric pH, preventing sucralfate polymerization
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ranitidine raises gastric pH, preventing sucralfate polymerization

 

Sucralfate is a cytoprotective agent that works by polymerizing in acidic conditions (pH < 4) to form a protective gel that adheres to the ulcer base. Ranitidine, being an H2 receptor blocker, reduces gastric acid secretion and raises gastric pH above 4. When gastric pH rises above 4, sucralfate cannot polymerize effectively, rendering it therapeutically ineffective. This represents a pharmacodynamic incompatibility where one drug's mechanism (acid suppression) interferes with another drug's mechanism (acid-dependent polymerization). Therefore, sucralfate should be given separately from acid-suppressing agents.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Ranitidine inhibits sucralfate absorption: This is not the mechanism. The issue is functional incompatibility, not absorption problems. 

 

Option B. Sucralfate increases ranitidine toxicity: Sucralfate does not significantly affect ranitidine's pharmacokinetics or increase its toxicity. 

 

Option D. The combination causes severe drug interactions: While the combination is irrational, it doesn't cause severe toxic interactions; it simply makes sucralfate ineffective.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Sucralfate requires acidic pH (< 4) for polymerization and effectiveness; concurrent use with acid-suppressing drugs like H2 blockers renders sucralfate ineffective.

The issue is functional incompatibility, not absorption problems. Option B. questions.stem: A patient with congestive heart failure is prescribed a drug that acts by inhibiting Na+-K+ ATPase pump, leading to increased intracellular calcium and improved myocardial contractility. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristic of toxicity from this drug?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Xanthopsia

 

The drug described is digitalis (digoxin), which acts by inhibiting the Na+-K+ ATPase pump. This inhibition leads to increased intracellular sodium, which in turn affects the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger, resulting in increased intracellular calcium and improved myocardial contractility. Yellow vision (xanthopsia) is a characteristic sign of digitalis toxicity, along with other visual disturbances, cardiac arrhythmias, nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Digitalis has a narrow therapeutic index, making toxicity a significant clinical concern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pulmonary fibrosis: This is characteristic of amiodarone toxicity, not digitalis toxicity.

 

Option B. Cinchonism: This syndrome (tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo, headache) is characteristic of quinidine toxicity.

 

Option D. Peripheral neuropathy: This can occur with amiodarone, isoniazid, or vincristine, but is not characteristic of digitalis toxicity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Digitalis toxicity characteristically presents with yellow-green vision (xanthopsia) along with cardiac arrhythmias and GI symptoms, due to Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old patient with Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia requires combination therapy. Which of the following combinations represents the treatment of choice?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ceftazidime + Amikacin

 

Ceftazidime plus aminoglycoside (such as amikacin) is the treatment of choice for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. This combination provides synergistic bactericidal activity. Ceftazidime is a third-generation cephalosporin with excellent anti-pseudomonal activity, while gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that enhances the killing effect. The combination helps prevent resistance development and improves clinical outcomes. Other anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams that can be used include piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, or meropenem, always in combination with an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vancomycin + Gentamicin: Vancomycin is not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa as it's a gram-negative organism and vancomycin only works against gram-positive bacteria.

 

Option C. Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin: Ceftriaxone has poor anti-pseudomonal activity, and this combination is more appropriate for community-acquired pneumonia.

 

Option D. Clindamycin + Ciprofloxacin: Clindamycin is ineffective against gram-negative organisms like Pseudomonas, though ciprofloxacin alone has anti-pseudomonal activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pseudomonas aeruginosa requires combination therapy with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (ceftazidime, piperacillin) plus aminoglycoside (gentamicin) or fluoroquinolone for optimal treatment.

questions.stem: The most common side effect of cancer chemotherapy is nausea with or without vomiting. The anticancer drugs vary is their ability to cause nausea and vomiting. Which of the following anti-cancer drugs is least likely to cause nausea and vomiting?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Chlorambucil

 

Among anticancer drugs, the likelihood of causing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) varies widely. Cisplatin is notorious for causing severe and prolonged emesis (highest emetogenic potential). Doxorubicin and daunorubicin also cause nausea and vomiting, though to a moderate degree. In contrast, chlorambucil is an oral alkylating agent that is generally well tolerated and least likely to cause significant nausea and vomiting, making it the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cisplatin: Platinum compound with very high emetogenic potential, often requiring prophylaxis with 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron), NK1 antagonists (aprepitant), and corticosteroids. One of the worst offenders for CINV.

 

Option C. Doxorubicin: Anthracycline antibiotic. Causes moderate nausea and vomiting; also cardiotoxicity (dose-dependent). Definitely more emetogenic than chlorambucil.

 

Option D. Daunorubicin: Another anthracycline, similar to doxorubicin, with moderate emetogenic potential and significant myelosuppression and cardiotoxicity. Not as bad as cisplatin but still more than chlorambucil.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Rituximab is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a humanised monoclonal antibody against CD-20

options.label: C
options.text: It is used for treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

options.label: D
options.text: Its most common adverse effect is infusion-related reactions

questions.answerText: It is a humanised monoclonal antibody against CD-20
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) It is a humanised monoclonal antibody against CD-20

 

Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody (murine + human) directed against CD20 antigen on B-lymphocytes. Humanised mAbs end with “-zumab” (e.g., Trastuzumab), while Rituximab (-ximab) indicates it is chimeric, not humanised.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. It has first-order kinetics: True. Rituximab shows first-order pharmacokinetics with elimination half-life prolonged after repeated dosing because of depletion of B-cells.

 

Option C. It is used for treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphoma: True. It is a standard drug in CD20-positive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, also used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatoid arthritis, and some autoimmune diseases.

 

Option D. Its most common adverse effect is infusion-related reactions: True. The most frequent ADRs are infusion-related reactions (fever, chills, hypotension, bronchospasm). They usually occur during the first infusion. Premedication with antihistamines and corticosteroids reduces severity.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is started on an intravenous monoclonal antibody therapy. Four months later, his liver function tests show: ALT: 325 U/LAST: 280 U/LTotal bilirubin: 3.2 mg/dL Viral hepatitis serologies are negative. A liver biopsy shows dense lymphocytic infiltration consistent with autoimmune hepatitis. Which of the following statements about the drug most likely responsible for this complication is true?

options.label: A
options.text: It blocks the PD-1 receptor on T-cells, preventing interaction with PD-L1 and enhancing antitumor activity

options.label: B
options.text: It mimics CTLA-4 to prevent co-stimulation of T-cells and is mainly used in rheumatoid arthritis

options.label: C
options.text: It depletes CD20-positive B lymphocytes and is commonly used in B-cell lymphomas

options.label: D
options.text: Its mechanism involves binding IL-2 receptor (CD25) to prevent T-cell proliferation, mainly used in transplant rejection prophylaxis

questions.answerText: It blocks the PD-1 receptor on T-cells, preventing interaction with PD-L1 and enhancing antitumor activity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) It blocks the PD-1 receptor on T-cells, preventing interaction with PD-L1 and enhancing antitumor activity

 

  • Drugs like Nivolumab, Pembrolizumab are PD-1 inhibitors. They prevent PD-1 receptor on T-cells from binding PD-L1 on tumor cells. This “releases the brakes” on T-cells, enhancing cytotoxic antitumor response.
  • Immune-related adverse events include autoimmune hepatitis, colitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis, hypophysitis.
  • Used in melanoma, NSCLC, RCC, Hodgkin lymphoma, head & neck SCC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. It mimics CTLA-4 to prevent co-stimulation of T-cells and is mainly used in rheumatoid arthritis: False. That’s Abatacept, a co-stimulation inhibitor for RA/autoimmune disease, not cancer. In contrast, Ipilimumabblocks CTLA-4 to enhance T-cell activation, but that’s not what’s described here.

 

Option C. It depletes CD20-positive B lymphocytes and is commonly used in B-cell lymphomas: False. That’s Rituximab, used in B-cell NHL, CLL, and autoimmune diseases. Its adverse effects are infusion reactionsand immunosuppression, not autoimmune hepatitis.

 

Option D. Its mechanism involves binding IL-2 receptor (CD25) to prevent T-cell proliferation, mainly used in transplant rejection prophylaxis: False. That’s Basiliximab, used in renal transplant rejection prophylaxis. Not related to NSCLC or autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stemHtml: A patient with head and neck cancer was given radiotherapy. After 6 months of radiotherapy, chemotherapy was started but patient presented with the clinical picture as shown after start of chemotherapy. What is the likely drug responsible for this?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Doxorubicin

 

  • Radiation recall syndrome = inflammatory reaction (erythema, edema, vesiculation, desquamation) that reappears in areas of prior radiotherapy after certain chemotherapy drugs.
  • Most commonly caused by anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin), but also by taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel) and gemcitabine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cyclophosphamide: False. Alkylating agent, causes hemorrhagic cystitis, bone marrow suppression, SIADH — but not classically associated with radiation recall.

 

Option C. Cisplatin: False. Platinum compound with high emetogenic potential, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy. Not linked to radiation recall.

 

Option D. Methotrexate: False. Can cause mucositis, hepatotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, myelosuppression. Rarely reported in recall, but not the classic cause (anthracyclines/taxanes are).

questions.stem: A 42-year-old patient with unstable angina is scheduled for percutaneous coronary intervention. An antiplatelet drug is chosen that directly binds to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on platelets. Which of the following agents works via this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Tirofiban

 

Tirofiban is a non-peptide, reversible antagonist of platelet GP IIb/IIIa receptors. This receptor is the final common pathway for platelet aggregation, and blocking it prevents binding of fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, thereby inhibiting platelet cross-linking. It is mainly used in acute coronary syndromes and during percutaneous coronary intervention to reduce thrombotic complications.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Prasugrel: An irreversible P2Y12 ADP receptor inhibitor, it prevents activation of GP IIb/IIIa receptors but does not directly block them.

 

Option B. Enoxaparin: A low molecular weight heparin that inhibits factor Xa; it is an anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet agent.

 

Option C. Fondaparinux: An indirect factor Xa inhibitor; it has anticoagulant effects but does not act on platelet aggregation directly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tirofiban directly blocks GP IIb/IIIa receptors, preventing fibrinogen binding and platelet aggregation, making it a potent antiplatelet agent used in ACS and PCI.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman, 2 years post-menopause, underwent a mastectomy and adjuvant radiotherapy for an invasive ductal carcinoma. Pathology revealed the tumor was strongly positive for estrogen receptors and negative for HER2 overexpression. She has no evidence of metastasis on imaging. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to reduce the risk of disease recurrence?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anastrozole

 

This postmenopausal woman has ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer after mastectomy + radiotherapy. The goal now is adjuvant endocrine therapy to reduce recurrence.

 

  • In premenopausal women, Tamoxifen (SERM) is usually preferred.
  • In postmenopausal women, aromatase inhibitors (AIs: Anastrozole, Letrozole, Exemestane) are superior to tamoxifen for recurrence prevention.

 

Thus, the best choice here is Anastrozole, an aromatase inhibitor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tamoxifen: Incorrect. SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator). Standard in premenopausal women, but in postmenopausal women, AIs are more effective for recurrence prevention. Still sometimes used if AIs are contraindicated (e.g., osteoporosis).

 

Option B. Trastuzumab: Incorrect. Monoclonal antibody against HER2/neu receptor. Indicated only in HER2-positive breast cancers. This patient’s tumor is HER2-negative, so trastuzumab has no role.

 

Option C. Fulvestrant: Incorrect. Pure ER antagonist (selective estrogen receptor degrader, SERD). Used mainly in metastatic, advanced, or tamoxifen-resistant ER+ breast cancer, not as first-line adjuvant therapy.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity presents for follow-up. Despite lifestyle modifications and metformin therapy, he has not achieved significant weight loss. The endocrinologist recommends initiating a medication that acts via the incretin pathway, reduces appetite, and improves glycemic control. Which of the following drugs best fits this profile?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Semaglutide

 

Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the effects of endogenous glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), an incretin hormone.

 

  • It enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release, and slows gastric emptying.
  • Importantly, it reduces appetite by acting on the hypothalamus, making it useful in weight reduction.
  • It has been shown to improve glycemic control and promote substantial weight loss in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Orlistat: Works by inhibiting pancreatic lipase, reducing fat absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. While it promotes weight loss, it does not act via the incretin system and has no direct appetite-suppressing central effects.

 

Option B. Octreotide: A somatostatin analog used for acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and variceal bleeding. It inhibits multiple gastrointestinal hormones but does not work on the incretin system for weight loss.

 

Option C. Nesiritide: A recombinant B-type natriuretic peptide used in acute decompensated heart failure to promote vasodilation and natriuresis. It has no role in appetite suppression or incretin modulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide promote weight loss by reducing appetite and slowing gastric emptying, in addition to improving glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, through activation of the incretin pathway.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female patient is undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer. The oncology team is concerned about the risk of febrile neutropenia due to the chemotherapeutic regimen. They are contemplating the use of a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and discuss the option of using pegylated-filgrastim or filgrastim. Which of the following is true about pegylated-filgrastim as compared to filgrastim?

options.label: A
options.text: Duration of action is longer than filgrastim

options.label: B
options.text: Added advantage is that it can be taken orally

options.label: C
options.text: Pegylated filgrastim is GM-CSF whereas filgrastim is G-CSF.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not effective in the treatment of severe neutropenia.

questions.answerText: Duration of action is longer than filgrastim
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Duration of action is longer than filgrastim.

 

Pegylated-filgrastim, also known as peg-filgrastim, is a long-acting formulation of filgrastim that is used to stimulate the production of white blood cells in patients receiving chemotherapy. The addition of polyethylene glycol (PEG) to filgrastim increases its molecular weight and slows down its clearance from the body, resulting in a longer duration of action compared to normal filgrastim.

 

Peg-filgrastim has a longer duration of action compared to regular filgrastim, requiring less frequent dosing.

 

Other Option:

 

Option B. Pegylated filgrastim: Is administered subcutaneously and is not available in oral form.

 

Option C. Both pegylated: Filgrastim and filgrastim are forms of G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). GM-CSF (granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor) is a different molecule.

 

Option D. Pegylated: Filgrastim is effective in the treatment of neutropenia and is often used to reduce the risk of infection in patients undergoing chemotherapy.

questions.stem: Which one of the following drugs is most effective in the treatment of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Methotrexate

 

Methotrexate is the first-line treatment for low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). It is highly effective, particularly in cases of non-metastatic or low-risk metastatic GTN. It works by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, which disrupts DNA synthesis and cell replication in rapidly dividing trophoblastic tissue. For high-risk GTN, combination chemotherapy regimens, which may include methotrexate, are used.
